title: NURS 1017 Unit 7 Case Study 3
description: 19-year-old university student with meningococcal meningitis and early sepsis: recognizing the hallmark signs of meningeal irritation, increased ICP and sepsis (including the nonblanching rash), nursing priorities, droplet precautions, a quiet environment, seizure precautions and public health follow-up, monitoring for vancomycin and dexamethasone adverse effects, care during and after a seizure, communicating hydrocephalus, and evaluation of complications such as hearing loss.

question.stem: The nurse reviews the client's history and assessment. Which of the following findings would be consistent with bacterial meningitis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Neck stiffness with pain on flexion

question.explanation:
Consistent with bacterial meningitis: fever, a severe headache and vomiting, and meningeal irritation: neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), photophobia, a positive Kernig sign (pain and resistance when the knee is extended with the hip flexed) and a positive Brudzinski sign (neck flexion causes flexion of the hips and knees). Inflamed meninges are stretched by these movements. Confusion and drowsiness reflect cerebral inflammation and rising ICP.

Also important: a nonblanching petechial rash, hypotension, tachycardia and poor perfusion point to meningococcemia (Neisseria meningitidis in the bloodstream), which can progress to septic shock within hours.

Not consistent: equal, reactive pupils, normal oxygen saturation, a soft abdomen and the menstrual history are expected or unrelated findings.

question.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether it is a sign of meningeal irritation, increased intracranial pressure (ICP), or sepsis. Each finding may be a sign of more than one problem.

rows.text: Neck stiffness with pain on flexion
Drowsy and oriented to person only
Nonblanching petechial rash on the legs and trunk
Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs
BP 96/58 mm Hg, cool hands and feet, and a capillary refill of 4 seconds
Photophobia
CSF opening pressure of 32 cm H₂O
Lactate 4.1 mmol/L

question.explanation:
How bacterial meningitis develops: Neisseria meningitidis spreads by respiratory droplets and close contact (shared residences). It colonizes the nasopharynx, enters the bloodstream, crosses the blood-brain barrier and multiplies in the CSF. The body's inflammatory response fills the space around the brain with white cells and pus (the cloudy CSF with neutrophils, high protein and low glucose on her results), irritates the meninges, and makes the brain swell.

Meningeal irritation (hallmark signs): neck stiffness, photophobia, and positive Kernig (pain and resistance when the knee is straightened with the hip flexed) and Brudzinski (bending the neck makes the hips and knees flex) signs, because these movements stretch the inflamed meninges.

Increased ICP: a falling level of consciousness is the earliest sign; the high CSF opening pressure confirms it. Swelling comes from leaky vessels (vasogenic edema), injured cells (cytotoxic edema) and blocked CSF absorption.

Sepsis: meningococcal bacteria in the blood cause low BP, poor perfusion (cool skin, slow capillary refill), a high lactate, and a nonblanching petechial or purpuric rash from bleeding into the skin as clotting factors and platelets are used up (platelets 88 × 10⁹/L). Drowsiness can come from both raised ICP and poor brain perfusion. The rash is a hallmark of meningococcal disease and must be reported at once.

question.stem: Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

cloze.text: The client is at highest risk for [[drop0]] as a result of [[drop1]]. She is also at risk for [[drop2]], as shown by [[drop3]].

options.text: demyelination of the central nervous system
cerebral edema from the inflammatory response
septic shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation
hypotension, a nonblanching rash, a high lactate, and a low platelet count

question.explanation:
Increased ICP from cerebral edema: the opening pressure of 32 cm H₂O and the falling level of consciousness show raised ICP. Meningitis causes all three types of cerebral edema: vasogenic (inflammation makes the blood-brain barrier leaky, so plasma moves into the brain's extracellular space), cytotoxic (toxins and ischemia make cell membrane pumps fail, so water moves into cells), and interstitial (purulent exudate blocks CSF absorption, causing hydrocephalus). Raised ICP can lead to herniation.

Septic shock and DIC: meningococcemia releases large amounts of endotoxin, causing vasodilation and capillary leak (BP 96/58 mm Hg, cool extremities, slow capillary refill, lactate 4.1 mmol/L) and widespread clotting that uses up platelets (88 × 10⁹/L) and clotting factors, causing the nonblanching petechial rash that can become purpura and skin necrosis.

Why not the others: photophobia and neck stiffness are meningeal signs, not signs of sepsis; the friend's cold is an exposure clue; the sodium is only slightly low. Autonomic dysreflexia, spinal and neurogenic shock follow spinal cord injury; demyelination is multiple sclerosis.

question.preamble: The nurse has reviewed the Provider Orders.
question.stem: Which interventions should the nurse include in the client's plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain droplet precautions until she has received 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy
Watch for flushing, itching and low BP during the vancomycin infusion
Keep the room quiet and dimly lit
Restrict fluids to 500 mL per day to prevent cerebral edema
Support the neck in flexion on two pillows to ease the neck pain
Elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees
Place her in a negative-pressure room and wear an N95 respirator for all care
Confirm that public health has been notified so close contacts can receive preventive antibiotics
Check her capillary glucose while she receives dexamethasone

question.explanation:
Include: N. meningitidis spreads by large respiratory droplets, so droplet precautions (surgical mask within 2 metres, private room) continue until 24 hours of effective therapy. A quiet, dim room eases photophobia and headache and avoids stimulation that can raise ICP. The head of the bed at 30 degrees aids venous drainage. Irritation of the brain surface makes seizures common, so seizure precautions are in place. Meningococcal disease is reportable: public health traces close contacts (roommates, partners, people who shared drinks) and arranges preventive antibiotics and vaccination.

Medication adverse effects: vancomycin infused too quickly can cause a vancomycin infusion reaction (flushing and itching of the face, neck and upper body, sometimes low BP); the nurse slows or stops the infusion and reports it. Vancomycin can also harm the kidneys, so creatinine and trough levels are followed. Dexamethasone raises blood glucose (and can cause gastric irritation, mood change and insomnia), so glucose is monitored.

Do not include: airborne precautions with a negative-pressure room are for diseases such as tuberculosis or measles, not meningococcus. Fluid restriction would worsen her shock; she needs fluids to maintain perfusion (sodium is monitored, because meningitis can cause water retention). Neck flexion is painful and can obstruct venous outflow from the head; the neck is kept in a neutral position.

Prevention: in Canada, the MenC-ACYW vaccine is given in the school program and the MenB vaccine to people at higher risk; both are part of the nurse's teaching for students in shared housing.

question.stem: For each action, click to specify whether it is indicated or contraindicated for the client at this time.

rows.text: Turn the client onto her side and suction the mouth as needed
Place a padded tongue blade between her teeth in case another seizure occurs
Apply oxygen and monitor her airway and breathing closely
Administer the levetiracetam loading dose
Prepare her for a repeat lumbar puncture to drain CSF and lower the pressure
Discontinue droplet precautions because she has received 8 hours of antibiotics
Prepare her for the STAT head CT

question.explanation:
Seizure classification (International League Against Epilepsy): seizures are focal onset (starting in one hemisphere; with awareness or with impaired awareness; may spread to a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure), generalized onset (both hemispheres from the start: motor, such as tonic-clonic, tonic, clonic, myoclonic and atonic, or non-motor, such as absence), or unknown onset. This seizure began with whole-body stiffening and jerking without focal signs, so it is described as a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. A seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or repeated seizures without recovery between them, is status epilepticus.

Indicated: after the seizure she is postictal with snoring respirations and SpO₂ 91%: a side-lying position and suction keep the airway clear, and oxygen is given. The loading dose of levetiracetam prevents further seizures. Her worsening headache, vomiting, falling GCS and Cushing's triad (widening pulse pressure, relative bradycardia, irregular breathing) signal rising ICP, so she goes for the STAT CT.

Contraindicated: nothing is placed in the mouth during a seizure (broken teeth, airway obstruction, bitten fingers). A lumbar puncture with suspected raised ICP can cause herniation. Droplet precautions continue until 24 hours of effective therapy.

question.explanation:
Hydrocephalus is an excess of CSF in the ventricles. In non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus, CSF flow is blocked within the ventricular system (for example, aqueductal stenosis, a tumor or a clot), so only the ventricles above the block enlarge. In communicating (non-obstructive) hydrocephalus, CSF flows through the ventricles but is not absorbed by the arachnoid villi (granulations), as after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage, so all ventricles enlarge, as in this client. Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating type in older adults with gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and dementia. The EVD drained CSF until absorption recovered.

Outcomes met: a normal level of consciousness without seizures, normal ventricles, a normal platelet count and lactate (DIC and shock resolved), no fever with a normal WBC (infection controlled), and close contacts treated to prevent secondary cases.

Require follow-up: sensorineural hearing loss is the most common lasting complication of bacterial meningitis (inflammation of the inner ear and cranial nerve VIII); she needs an urgent audiology assessment, because early treatment, including cochlear implants, matters. Dark, dry skin on the toes suggests necrosis from the clotting in small vessels during meningococcemia and needs wound care assessment.
